findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete for all 5 Roland rhythm-machine instruments (cr78, tr606, tr707, tr808, tr909) -- 2-4 sources visited per instrument this session, license called per source, voice structure sourced and compared to each module's MAX_VOICES.

Durable method discoveries for future Station A work on classic Roland gear (would go in docs/agent-knowledge/instrument-sources.md under normal rules; recorded here only per this run's no-files override):

1. Internet Archive reliably hosts scanned Roland service notes under predictable identifiers -- "synthmanual-roland-<model>-service-notes" worked for cr78, tr606, tr808; "roland_Roland_TR-909_Service_Manual" / "manualzz-id-*" for tr909. None of these items carry an explicit rights/licenseurl field in their metadata (checked via https://archive.org/metadata/<id> for four of the five this session) -- treat every one as "license unverified" by default. synthxl.com's mirror of the same class of manual is the one place an explicit (if restrictive) license line was actually found: "collected from the World Wide Web...may not be used for any commercial purposes" -- a useful phrase to search page text for when trying to firm up a license call on a scanned manual.

2. dafx.de's own paper-archive (e.g. https://www.dafx.de/paper-archive/2014/...) serves PDFs directly and reliably (confirmed 200 OK, 4.2MB via curl) where an institutional mirror can 403 (pure.qub.ac.uk did, this session). Go to the official DAFx archive first, not a university repository mirror.

3. oramics.github.io/sampled (repo: github.com/oramics/sampled) is a small but genuinely Public-Domain-licensed library of real hardware drum-machine samples, with an explicit per-instrument license statement on each instrument's own page (distinct from the site's own MIT-licensed code). Worth checking first for any classic drum machine survey -- it was the cleanest license call reached this session, cleaner than several commercial "free" packs whose pages state no terms at all.

4. The signature to search for when hunting known-settings captures (vision §4 / roadmap D3) is knob values embedded directly in sample filenames -- e.g. audiorealism.se's TR-909 pack ("BassDrum909-tune050-attack100-decay100.wav"). This was the only clean known-settings source found across 5 instrument families this session (1 of 5); everything else was pack-level/statistical. That ratio is itself evidence for D3: known-settings captures exist but are rare, so a dossier should default to characterizing across a pack (statistical envelope) unless a filename-encoded or explicitly-documented source like audiorealism.se's turns up for that specific instrument.

5. Marketing/promo copy for an open-source project can overstate its derivation -- audiokitpro.com's page for the "Super 606" DSP claims circuit analysis by a named engineer, but the linked repo's own README describes itself only as "an independent project inspired by classic analog drum-machine circuits for learning and education purposes," with no such claim. Always read the repo's own README, not the vendor's landing page, before crediting a methodology in a dossier.

6. A caution surfaced by tr707: not every "circuit-derived model from literature" tier-2 source applies cleanly to every instrument. The TR-707 (and any other ROM/PCM-sample-playback machine, as opposed to an analog voice circuit) has no interesting circuit nonlinearity for a DAFx-style paper to model -- none was found, and none should be expected. For romplers, the literature tier's useful content is the ROM/CPU architecture (chip part numbers, sample bit-depth, channel count) rather than circuit equations, and the natural tier-1 reference is a hardware capture or, ideally, an actual ROM dump (not searched for this session -- worth a dedicated hunt at dossier time).

findings.method_notes:
Phase 0 survey, sample-based/analog drum-machine family (linndrum, dmx, drumtraks, sp1200, simmons_sdsv). All work was findings-only per this run's override: no files written, no dossiers drafted, module code read only far enough to corroborate the MAX_VOICES facts already supplied in the brief (grep -n confirmed: linndrum.py:118, dmx.py:134, simmons_sdsv.py:99 each declare MAX_VOICES = 16; drumtraks.py and sp1200.py declare no module-level MAX_VOICES at all).

Durable method discoveries for docs/agent-knowledge/instrument-sources.md (not written this run per the override - Brad or a future run should fold these in):

1. archive.org's metadata API (https://archive.org/metadata/<identifier>) is the fast, reliable way to check an item's actual license: request it and look at the "licenseurl" field. Most vintage-manual scans on archive.org carry NO licenseurl/rights field at all (treat as license-unverified/default terms), but when an uploader does set one it shows up clean and unambiguous - e.g. the E-mu SP-1200 Service Manual is explicitly tagged CC Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://archive.org/metadata/emu-sp-1200-service-manual-1987_202010). Always check the metadata endpoint, not just the item page, since the rendered page frequently omits the rights line entirely.

2. A recurring red flag on archive.org's "Community Audio" collection: items titled after a specific drum machine (e.g. "Oberheim DMX Drums - Stock DMX Sounds", "E-mu SP-1200 Drums - Turbo Kit") both carried the identical boilerplate description "Custom Fairlight CMI sample pack NN" - completely mismatched with their titles. This is the signature of a single uploader's batch-uploaded, likely mislabeled or repurposed generic pack collection. Treat any Community Audio item from this pattern as unverified provenance regardless of its title, and check the description field via the metadata API before citing one.

3. elektrotanya.com is a broad, reliable archive of classic drum-machine/synth service manuals and schematics (Linn, Oberheim, Sequential, Simmons all present) - useful for the literature tier - but its site-wide terms state personal-use-only download ("please do not offer the downloaded file for sell only use it for personal usage"), confirmed by direct page visit. That's consistent with reading for circuit-behavior derivation, never for republishing the scan.

4. The bar that actually separates a usable ("gold") hardware capture from the rest, observed across this whole family: an established sample house that (a) states its capture chain (mic/preamp/tape path) and (b) documents a hardware-parameter sweep (Samples From Mars' SP-1200 pack: "multi-sampling every hit with 16 SP tunings") and (c) publishes a real Terms & Conditions page (not just "free download"). Of the five hardware-capture candidates actually reached this run, only one (Samples From Mars, SP-1200) cleared all three; every "free from the internet"/community-audio pack found for the other four instruments failed at least one, usually (b) and often (c) as well. This is direct evidence toward the roadmap's D3 question: known-settings captures are NOT common in this drum family outside of a small number of reputable commercial sample houses - a statistical/characterize-across-a-pack approach is likely to be the honest default rule for most of the 53 instruments, with known-settings captures the exception rather than the norm.

5. Two WebFetch attempts (samplefocus.com, reverb.com) returned HTTP 403 this run; both were treated as dead/unusable per evidence discipline rather than cited from memory or from WebSearch snippets about them.

findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete for the Moog/ARP monosynth family (minimoog, taurus, arp2600, odyssey) — 3-4 sources visited per instrument across capture/literature/oss tiers, license called per source, voice structure confirmed against MAX_VOICES for all four. No dossiers written, no files written (per this run's override).

Durable method discoveries worth keeping for other Station A researchers:

1. GitHub API license verification is far more reliable than reading a repo's rendered page. `curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo> | grep -A3 '"license"'` returns GitHub's own SPDX-verified license classification, and `.../contents/` lists files to confirm a LICENSE file actually exists. This caught a real discrepancy: a WebFetch of zynthian/moog's page initially attributed 'MIT' to page-footer text ambiguously; the API confirmed it against the actual LICENSE.md. It also cleanly confirmed a negative (joanrieu/synth-odyssey and rhaamo/ARP-2600 have no license field and no LICENSE file — treat as unlicensed/all-rights-reserved per the gate's default rule). Caveat: the unauthenticated search endpoint (`/search/repositories`) rate-limits hard (a handful of calls/minute) — space calls out or accept silent empty results (a rate-limit error JSON has no 'items' key, so naive parsing silently returns nothing, which looks identical to 'no results found' — always check for a 'message' field first).

2. archive.org's `/metadata/<identifier>` JSON endpoint is the reliable way to check for `licenseurl`/`rights`/`possible-copyright-status` on scanned service manuals, and is far more informative than WebFetching the item page. Across five scanned OEM manuals checked this run (Minimoog, ARP 2600, ARP Odyssey original, Korg ARP Odyssey reissue, plus the general pattern), none carried an explicit rights statement — the honest default for this whole class of source is 'license unverified, presumed all-rights-reserved, read for circuit-derived literature only' rather than any positive license claim.

3. Classic Moog/ARP sample packs are plentiful but consistently under-document both license terms and capture settings: of the eight capture-pack pages visited across this family (Monosounds, Wave Alchemy, Freesound, Samples From Mars, Cyborg Studio, BØLT), only one (Monosounds) stated usable license terms directly on the product page, and *none* documented the oscillator/filter/patch settings used per sample. This is real evidence toward the roadmap's D3 question: known-settings captures are not common in this family, and a statistical/typical-patch envelope is the honest default, not an exception.

4. Huovilainen's 'Non-Linear Digital Implementation of the Moog Ladder Filter' (DAFx 2004, https://dafx.de/paper-archive/2004/P_061.PDF) is a reusable literature anchor for *any* instrument sharing the Moog 4-pole ladder VCF — used here for both minimoog and taurus — worth remembering across the whole Moog corpus (and any other module using a Moog-style ladder filter), not just these four instruments.

5. Two dead ends worth flagging so nobody re-spends time: bigfishaudio.com product pages return HTTP 403 to automated fetches; PDF rendering via the Read tool requires poppler-utils (`pdftoppm`), which is not installed in this environment, so image-based scanned PDFs (common for 1970s service manuals) can be fetched but not visually inspected this run.

findings.method_notes:
Durable method discoveries from this survey, worth keeping for future Station A work on other families:

1. Internet Archive's "synthmanual-*" and manufacturer-service-manual items reliably serve scanned OEM service manuals/schematics for classic Roland/Korg gear (search pattern: "<brand> <model> service manual archive.org"). These item pages consistently carry no explicit reuse license — treat uniformly as "license unverified / standard copyright presumed," safe to read for circuit-topology derivation per the vision's literature-tier rule, never to redistribute.

2. dafx.de/paper-archive is the primary index for DAFx circuit-modeling papers, but raw paper PDF URLs frequently fail to text-extract via WebFetch (return only unreadable binary/compressed content). When that happens, the paper's own metadata/abstract mirror page — dafx.de/paper-archive/details.php?id=..., or a university repository page like research.aalto.fi/en/publications/... — reliably returns readable title/authors/venue/abstract even when the raw PDF does not. Worth trying the mirror first for any DAFx citation.

3. Csound's opcode manual (csound.com/docs/manual/<opcode>.html) documents the source literature (author, app note, textbook) behind many of its virtual-analog models — a fast route to the underlying circuit-derivation paper for a given filter type. Example: K35_lpf/K35_hpf point straight to Will Pirkle's AN-5/AN-7 app notes and Vadim Zavalishin's "Art of VA Filter Design" for the Korg35 filter used in the MS-10/early MS-20. Csound itself is LGPL-2.1-or-later (confirmed at github.com/csound/csound/blob/develop/COPYING) — copyleft, so its own code is a proxy-output oracle only, never ported; the papers it cites are the actual literature-tier source and are worth chasing down separately.

4. Buchla is an outlier in the schematic-availability sense compared to Roland/Korg/EDP: no publicly archived circuit schematics were found for the Music Easel/208 (buchla.com/download/ ships only manuals and MIDI implementation docs). For Buchla-family (and likely other boutique/modular) gear where official schematics don't exist, DAFx literature on specific reusable circuit blocks (the vactrol low-pass gate; the 259 wavefolder) is the strongest tier-2 lever available even when it targets a sibling module rather than the exact instrument in question — the bridge from sibling-module paper to target instrument must be stated as an inference, not asserted as sourced fact.

5. Sample-pack product pages (Bandcamp, Gumroad, Loopmasters) almost never state a formal license; the operative signal is the specific product page's own text ("royalty-free," "Creative Commons," or Bandcamp's silent "all rights reserved" default). A marketing blurb, YouTube title, or forum thread describing a pack is not itself the license — fetch the actual product/download page every time.

6. Across this whole family, even the best-documented hardware-capture packs (TB-303's Loopmasters and OXIDE Sound Lab entries) only give categorical settings (envelope/filter "different per instrument," or filter fixed at three named percentages) rather than an exact per-sample knob log. This supports treating a statistical/characterization envelope, not a strict known-exact-settings requirement, as the workable Phase 0 rule for D3 — at least for this instrument family.

7. Reissue/clone provenance is a real trap for this family specifically: MS-20 sample packs in particular do not reliably state whether they were captured from an original analog MS-20 or the MS-20 Mini (a digital reissue) — worth a standing caution whenever a capture pack's hardware identity isn't explicit, since for MS-20 the difference is not cosmetic (different circuit implementation).

findings.method_notes: Internet Archive's 'synthmanuals' collection (all four schematic/service-manual sources above came from it, uploader sketch@cow.net) is a reliable first stop for OEM service manuals/schematics on classic synths — search 'archive.org details <machine> service manual'. Its item pages never show an explicit rights/licenseurl field for these scans in any of the four cases checked; the fast way to confirm this is https://archive.org/metadata/<identifier> (JSON), rather than screen-scraping the details page. Default finding: 'license unverified, manufacturer copyright presumed on the scan' — usable for circuit-derivation reading only, never for redistributing the PDF. electricdruid.net is a useful chip-level supplement when a manual is schematic-only and light on discussion (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, stated at each article's footer) — it covers CEM/SSM filter-chip topology shared across many 1980s machines and was independently useful for both prophet5 and obxa here. Mature OSS synth-emulator projects cluster on GPLv3 by default (OB-Xd through v2.11, Odin2 confirmed directly; Surge XT and Vaporizer2 confirmed via search only, not fetched this run) — expect this license going in and budget for measured-output-only use, never porting. instruments.hardware_voices: Paraphonic, not a fixed N-voice architecture: tone generation spans the full keyboard range (top-octave-divider style, no per-note voice limit) but sections share a single amplitude/filter envelope. 7 bandpass filters serve human-voice/choir tones (4 choir voicings drawing from a shared pool of 7), 10 bandpass filters serve the vocoder, and a stereo BBD ensemble (2 BBDs per channel, 4 total) provides the chorus.
instruments.structure_verdict: A mismatch in kind, not just count: the hardware is paraphonic with essentially unlimited note generation and a shared envelope, not a conventional N-independent-voice polyphonic synth. Module MAX_VOICES=4 imposes exactly the kind of per-note independent-voice cap the real VP-330 never had. This is a genuine finding for the dossier to resolve — whether 4 is a deliberate approximation of paraphony (audioif's voice-stealing model has no native paraphonic primitive) or should be revisited is Station B's/Brad's call, not mine, but the reference does not describe 4 discrete voices.

findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete for all five instruments (jupiter8, juno106, jp8000, d50, vp330) — 2–4 sources visited per instrument across the hierarchy tiers, per-source license calls made, hardware voice structure recorded against each module's MAX_VOICES, no dossiers written, no files written (per this run's override).

Durable method discoveries worth keeping for future source hunts:

1. Internet Archive's "synthmanual-roland-<model>-<doc-type>" slug pattern (e.g. synthmanual-roland-juno-106-service-notes, synthmanual-roland-vp-330-owners-manual) reliably serves scanned vintage Roland service notes and owner's manuals and was the single most productive literature-tier source across all five instruments this run. However, older-style numeric/catalog item IDs from the same "john-leimseider-archive" collection (e.g. JL11426 for the Jupiter-8 service manual) are unstable — the ID appeared correctly in search results and even in the collection's own metadata, but 404'd on direct fetch twice. Prefer the "synthmanual-*" slug when both exist. No archive.org manual page in this survey showed an explicit rights/license statement beyond a generic site Terms-of-Service link — treat every archive.org manual as license unverified by default (fine for literature-tier reading/circuit-derivation per vision §4/§5, never for redistribution).

2. WebFetch frequently cannot extract readable text from academic-thesis-style PDFs (returns raw/garbled binary), even though the underlying tool silently saves the downloaded PDF to the session's tool-results scratch path. When that happens, a local Python venv with `pip install pypdf` (works without --break-system-packages inside a venv) reliably extracts full text from that same saved file — this recovered two otherwise-unreadable sources this run (the Szabo and Shore Supersaw theses) and is worth reaching for before giving up on a PDF-only paper or manual.

3. ModWiggler forum thread pages return 403 Forbidden to WebFetch (apparent bot-blocking) — don't spend a fetch on modwiggler.com directly; get the same information via a WebSearch snippet or, better, the underlying project's own repo/site (this run: the actual JP8-4-ALL project turned out to be hosted on GitLab with its own license, reachable directly).

4. GitHub/GitLab repository root pages reliably surface a license badge or README license section without needing to open the raw LICENSE file — fast for per-source license triage in this program.

5. Freesound.org states an explicit per-upload Creative Commons license (this run: a real CC0 JP-8000 sample) — a genuinely open, verifiable license, unusually strong for a hardware-capture source in this hierarchy and worth checking early for any single-hit/one-shot hunt, drum machines included.

findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete for all four Korg-family instruments (polysix, ms2000, nord_lead, virus) — each graded with 3 visited sources and a sourced hardware-voice comparison against the module's MAX_VOICES. No dossiers drafted, no files written, per this run's overrides.

Durable method discoveries worth keeping for future Station A runs:

1. **archive.org's Korg service-manual holdings are reliable.** Individual `Korg_<model>_ServiceManual` items (confirmed working for Polysix and MS2000 this run) plus the broader `korg_service_manuals` collection consistently serve real factory service manuals with actual circuit-diagram sections, not just owner's manuals. None carry an explicit rights statement on the item page — default to "license unverified / publisher-copyright, read for engineering derivation only" for any Korg service manual pulled from there. ManualsLib mirrors the same manuals and is useful for confirming table-of-contents contents (it lists section headers even before download).

2. **dsp56300/gearmulator (github.com/dsp56300/gearmulator, GPL-3.0, confirmed at the repo) is a program-wide asset, not a one-off.** It's a cycle/IC-accurate emulator of the actual Motorola DSP56300 chip used across a wide swath of mid-90s/2000s virtual-analog hardware: Nord Lead 2/3, Access Virus A/B/C/TI/TI2, Waldorf Q/Microwave II, Novation Supernova (per its own docs). It runs the ORIGINAL firmware ROM rather than modeling behavior, so its output is close to bit-exact — about as strong a tier-3 proxy oracle as exists, and it will resurface for other instrument families in this program (Waldorf, Novation) whenever they're surveyed. Caveat that should be flagged upward rather than solved silently: using it for real requires a legitimate ROM dump of each target synth, which this run did not attempt to obtain — that's a program-level acquisition/legality question, not a research one.

3. **electricdruid.net is a solid literature-tier resource for classic synth-chip circuits** (SSM2044 and similar filter/oscillator ICs used across many vintage machines) but is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial) — fine to read for engineering derivation of math, not for redistributing its text or diagrams.

4. **Watch for freeware-but-closed-source "tribute" plugins polluting OSS searches.** MOODYSIX, Eightysix, Kp6 (Polysix), Synth1 (Nord Lead 2-inspired) all surface under searches like "open source X emulator" but none publish source code or a license file — confirmed by checking directly rather than trusting search-snippet phrasing. Only count something at the OSS/proxy tier after visiting its own repo/license page this run.

5. **License-unverified sample packs are the norm, not the exception**, for small studios and forum posts (Cyborg Studio, the Elektronauts Virus B pack) — "free download" or a creator's offhand claim of hardware provenance is not a license and not verified provenance; both were excluded from grading per the standing rule rather than assumed permissive.

findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete for all three Yamaha instruments (cs80, dx7, fs1r) — each graded, every grade sourced, every source's license read and recorded with the URL where it was read, per-instrument voice structure compared against MAX_VOICES. No files written (per this run's override); this response is the deliverable.

Durable method notes for the knowledge module (not written to disk this run, per override — Brad or a future Station A run should fold these into docs/agent-knowledge/instrument-sources.md):

1. **Freesound.org individual sound pages, not just pack pages, carry the real license and settings.** Pack-level pages (e.g. .../packs/29627/) often show no license text at all; the license (and often a settings dump: synth model, preset name, MIDI note, velocity) lives on each sound's own page (e.g. .../sounds/526634/). Always drill into at least one individual sound page before grading a Freesound pack — the pack page alone will underrate or overrate the source.

2. **Yamaha hosts its own owner's manuals at data.yamaha.com** (usa.yamaha.com download links 301-redirect there), and for the FS1R at least the manual is a genuine, detailed technical document — parameter charts, algorithm structure, spectral-form tables — not just a quick-start guide. For digital/FM-family Yamaha instruments (dx-series, tx-series, sy-series) this first-party PDF archive is likely to be the strongest single literature source available, worth checking before third-party manual-scan sites. WebFetch alone returns only a binary-PDF description for these; a throwaway venv with `pip install pypdf` (built in the scratchpad, not the repo) was enough to extract real text and search it by keyword — worth repeating for other instruments' official PDFs rather than settling for the page-description fallback.

3. **A GPL-licensed emulator repo can still contain a permissively-licensed core.** Dexed (github.com/asb2m10/dexed) is GPLv3 at the top level, but its vendored FM engine directory (Source/msfa/*, originally Google's "music-synthesizer-for-android") carries its own Apache-2.0 header in every file — confirmed by fetching a raw source file directly, not by trusting the README's summary. Before writing off a whole repo as copyleft, grep the specific engine files' own headers; some projects mix licenses per-subdirectory and the more permissive piece may be exactly the algorithm core needed.

4. **Manual-scan archives (therogoffs.com, elektrotanya.com, scribd) reliably serve service manuals/schematics for classic gear but almost never state a real license** — elektrotanya explicitly restricts to "personal usage," therogoffs.com states only a bare copyright name with no terms. Treat these uniformly as license-unverified/no-redistribution and read them only for circuit-derivation math (vision §4 tier 2), never as a source to port or even open verbatim if a first-party (manufacturer-hosted) manual covers the same ground — the manufacturer source is both more authoritative and easier to defend on license grounds (a clean ©-year copyright notice beats "license unverified").

5. **Watch for General-MIDI-style relabeling on general sample sites.** Free Wave Samples names its FS1R samples by an imitated instrument category and GM program number (e.g. "Accordion (#22)") rather than by the source synth's actual patch/algorithm name — a trap for assuming "settings documented" just because a plausible-looking label is present. Check what the label is actually naming before crediting known_settings=true.

findings.method_notes:
Durable method discoveries from this run, worth keeping for future Station A work (per this run's instructions, recorded here rather than in docs/agent-knowledge/instrument-sources.md since this run wrote no files):

1. **archive.org's advancedsearch.php JSON API is far more reliable than its search UI for WebFetch.** The human search page (archive.org/search?query=...) renders via JS and returns nothing useful to WebFetch. Instead query `https://archive.org/advancedsearch.php?q=title%3A%28TERMS%29&fl[]=identifier&fl[]=title&fl[]=mediatype&rows=20&output=json` -- a static JSON response WebFetch parses cleanly. This is how every archive.org schematic/service-manual/capture item in this survey was actually located (not via WebSearch, which never surfaced the exact archive.org identifiers).

2. **archive.org's per-item metadata API (`https://archive.org/metadata/<identifier>`) is the fastest way to make the license call.** It exposes `licenseurl`/`rights` fields directly; when both are absent (the near-universal case across every synth-manual and demo-audio item checked this run: PPG, Waldorf, Casio, Fairlight, E-mu, Kurzweil), that is a clean, citable "license unverified" finding rather than a guess -- record the metadata URL as `license_read_at`.

3. **`gh search repos "<term>"` (with `--json fullName,description,url,license`) is a solid, budget-cheap substitute for WebSearch when hunting OSS emulators/tools**, and it returns the SPDX license directly without a follow-up fetch in most cases. It surfaced several sources WebSearch missed entirely (avr-ppg, Waveset-Emulation, the EmulatorIIDemos capture, psobot/k2000).

4. **Low-level chip/firmware emulators (MAME cores, gearmulator/DSP56300 LLE) that run a machine's *original ROM* are an unusually strong proxy-oracle tier** -- stronger than a typical "modeled" GPL synth, because their output should be close to bit-accurate to the digital portion of the real signal chain. They are still GPL in the cases found (gearmulator, MAME core) and still gated the same way: measure output only, never port. Worth actively hunting for on any digital-engine instrument (Fairlight's MAME-based `fairlightCMI` setup and Waldorf's `gearmulator`/Xenia both fit this pattern).

5. **vintagesynth.com model-page URLs are not predictable by slug guessing** (e.g. `/emu/emulator-2`, `/fairlight/cmi-2x`, `/emu/emulator-ii` all 404'd) even though `/casio/cz-101`, `/kurzweil/k2600`, `/ppg/wave-2`, and `/waldorf/microwave` worked. No reliable index/sitemap page was found this run (`/emu` and `/fairlight` also 404'd) -- Wikipedia's spec tables are a fallback that worked consistently for voice-count facts when vintagesynth's slug guess failed.

6. **This session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) is shared and can be exhausted mid-task by other concurrent agents** -- it ran out partway through this six-instrument survey with no warning beyond the tool's own error message. WebFetch (to guessed or discovered URLs) and `gh search`/`gh api` remained available throughout and carried the back half of this survey. Future Station A work should front-load WebSearch calls per instrument or budget for this failure mode.

No dedicated hardware-capture library serving reliably documented single-note-at-known-settings captures was found for any of the six wavetable/PD/sampler/workstation instruments in this family -- every capture source located (PPG demos/packs, Fairlight factory library, Emulator II demo record, K2600 StudioSamples pack) had real or plausible hardware provenance but zero documented per-capture settings, and none had an explicit redistribution license. This is a real data point toward roadmap D3 (Q1: known-settings captures vs. a statistical envelope) -- for this family specifically, a statistical/aggregate-envelope approach looks like the honest path unless a dedicated hunt turns up a calibrated capture library Station A hasn't found yet.

findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete — all 5 electromechanical-piano instruments graded, 2-4 sources visited each, 15 sources total, license read (or explicitly recorded as unverified) at every one.

Session note: the WebSearch tool's budget was exhausted partway through this run (after ~9 calls, on the Wurlitzer hunt) with the message "this session has used its web search budget (200 of 200 WebSearch calls)" — evidently a session-wide, not per-agent-call, counter that had little headroom left when this survey started. All source-hunting after that point used two substitute methods, both worth keeping for future Station A work:

1. **GitHub's REST search API via curl, no auth needed** — `https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=<terms>` for candidate OSS emulators/capture-packs-as-repos, then `https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/license` for the SPDX-identified license, then `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch>/LICENSE` (or README) to actually read the license text and confirm content (e.g. via the contents API for sample-file listings). This was faster and more reliable than WebSearch/WebFetch for OSS license triage and turned up every OSS/pack source in this survey (elk-audio/mda-vst2, hal0zer0/openwurli, sfzinstruments/GregSullivan.E-Pianos, sgossner/VCSL, thecowgoesmoo/TwinCl, edwin-oetelaar/CP70_preamp). Recommended as the default first move for any OSS/pack hunt, independent of WebSearch budget.

2. **Bing's `format=rss` endpoint via curl is NOT reliable and should not be used** — it appears to do aggressive brand/entity matching: queries containing a recognizable brand name or short token (Hohner, Wurlitzer, Yamaha, CP-70 read as "CP") return generic corporate/navigational results for that entity and silently ignore the rest of the query, with no error signal. It produced junk for several queries in this run before being abandoned in favor of WebFetch on directly-guessed URLs. Google and DuckDuckGo were also tried and blocked (search-result pages, CAPTCHA). If WebSearch is unavailable, the practical fallback is WebFetch against specific guessed/known URLs (see below), not a scraped search engine.

3. **freesound.org pack pages don't reliably render per-file license/links via WebFetch's default extraction** — the fix is to explicitly prompt WebFetch to extract href patterns matching `/people/<user>/sounds/<id>/` from the pack page's raw HTML, then fetch one of those individual sound pages, which does reliably show the CC license variant and the uploader's description (which often documents the hardware model and signal chain — the closest thing to 'known settings' most captures offer).

4. **www.clavinet.com** (a Clavinet/Pianet spare-parts vendor site, guessed path `/schematics.php`) directly serves original Hohner Clavinet D6 and six Pianet-variant (C/L/M/N/N-v2/CH-amp/Combo) schematic PDFs — a genuine literature-tier archive worth returning to for any Hohner-family instrument.

5. **elektrotanya.com** (repair/e-waste-reduction community archive, URL pattern `elektrotanya.com/<manufacturer>_<model>.pdf/download.html`, guessable from manufacturer+model) confirmed a real Yamaha CP-70/CP-80/CP-60 service manual and parts list, with page-preview thumbnails visible before its click-through download gate. Worth trying for other manufacturer/model literature hunts, though full-text download is gated and was not completed here.

6. **sfzinstruments GitHub org** mirrors classic freeware SFZ multisample libraries with original licenses preserved (found Rhodes, Pianet T, Wurlitzer EP200, and CP80 all under one repo, `sfzinstruments/GregSullivan.E-Pianos`, CC BY 3.0) — a good first stop for electromechanical-keyboard captures specifically.

7. **sgossner/VCSL** (Versilian Community Sample Library, CC0-1.0 confirmed via GitHub API) is a zero-friction-license capture library worth checking first for any instrument; it did not cover any of this batch's five instruments but its Aerophones/Chordophones/Electrophones/Idiophones/Membranophones category structure is worth a look for other families (e.g. drums, synths).

Cross-cutting Phase-0-relevant finding, not instrument-specific: all five electromechanical pianos surveyed here are documented as 'full polyphony' hardware (Wikipedia technical-specs boxes, cited per-instrument) — each key/string/reed is an independent, non-stealing voice, with the only ceiling being the physical key count (60 to 88 depending on instrument). Every module's MAX_VOICES (16 for four of the five, 12 for cp70) sits well under that reference ceiling in all five cases, consistently in the same direction. That consistency across an entire family may be worth flagging to Brad at Gate 0 as a pattern rather than five isolated findings.

findings.method_notes:
Web search quota: this session's WebSearch budget (200 calls, apparently shared/cumulative across the environment rather than reset per sub-task) was exhausted partway through the survey, after b3's three sources. All four remaining instruments (farfisa, vox_continental, solina, mellotron) were surveyed entirely via WebFetch against known-URL archives instead — this worked well and is worth carrying forward as a fallback pattern for future Station A runs:

- **archive.org's JSON search API** (`https://archive.org/advancedsearch.php?q=<terms>&fl[]=identifier&fl[]=title&output=json&rows=N`) is a fast, reliable WebFetch target for hunting service manuals/schematics without WebSearch — cleaner than fetching the HTML search-results page, which sometimes rendered no results even when items exist. Follow with `https://archive.org/details/<identifier>` to read the item's own rights statement, which is frequently absent (most contributed manuals show no explicit license — expect "license unverified" to be the common outcome for this archive, not the exception).
- **GitHub license checks**: `curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>` and read the `.license.spdx_id` field — faster and more reliable than WebFetch on the repo's HTML page, which sometimes reported a "LICENSE file exists" without naming the license. When the API reports `null`/`"Other"`/`NOASSERTION`, fetch the raw file directly (`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch>/LICENSE`) before concluding "unverified" — in one case (Ho-Ro/connie) the raw file resolved a GitHub-API "Other" into a clear GPL-3.0 statement.
- **Freesound license checks**: a bare pack page (`/people/<user>/packs/<id>/`) frequently does NOT render the license badge to WebFetch (JS-dependent), but the **grouped search-results page** (`/search/?q=<terms>&g=1`) reliably shows an inline "License: <name>" label per pack/sound in the results list. Prefer the search view over the pack page when confirming a Freesound license.
- **PDF text extraction**: WebFetch cannot parse a fetched PDF's binary content directly (returns raw stream garbage) but does save the binary to a local tool-results path. `pdftotext`/`pdftoppm` (poppler-utils) were not installed and `apt-get` required sudo; a scratch venv (`python3 -m venv` + `pip install pypdf`) reliably extracted title/author/abstract text from a locally-saved DAFx PDF in under a minute and is worth reaching for by default rather than debugging poppler installation.
- DAFx conference papers are commonly hosted at conference-specific subdomains (e.g. `dafx16.vutbr.cz/dafxpapers/...`) rather than a single central archive; they carry no explicit license/CC statement in the PDF itself (standard academic copyright applies) but their math is citable per the program's literature-reading policy regardless.
- For hardware whose reference *is* a tape/sample library by nature (Mellotron), a note-labeled, CC0, single-note Freesound pack is about as strong a "capture" as this class of instrument can offer, even without an explicit "recorded from unit #X" provenance statement — worth treating as a legitimate gold candidate while flagging the provenance thinness honestly, rather than downgrading reflexively for the format.

instruments.hardware_voices: Not one hardware synthesizer -- Karplus-Strong is a DSP algorithm (Karplus & Strong 1983, extended by Jaffe & Smith 1983) most naturally modeling a single plucked string. Its most common physical referent, a standard guitar, has 6 strings (confirmed by the UIowa capture set's per-file string labels: E, A, D, G, B, high E) and is playable as a 6-note chord/strum, i.e. up to 6-voice polyphony for a guitar-shaped instantiation of the algorithm.

There is no single documented 'Karplus-Strong reference machine' polyphony spec to check this against, but the algorithm's most natural physical referent -- a standard 6-string guitar, per the capture set's own string list -- is itself 6-voice-capable, so MAX_VOICES=6 is a defensible match to that referent. This is inference from the plucked-string analog, not a cited hardware polyphony number, and should be flagged as such rather than treated as a confirmed hardware fact.
instruments.not_found: No single canonical 'Karplus-Strong hardware instrument' exists to check MAX_VOICES against directly -- the algorithm was first demonstrated on general-purpose DSP hardware and was licensed to Mattel Electronics for a toy (reportedly the 'Digital Music Synthesizer' patent licensing), but that toy's polyphony spec was not located this run. Did not reach the original 1983 Computer Music Journal paper itself (Karplus & Strong, 'Digital Synthesis of Plucked-String and Drum Timbres') -- it appears to be JSTOR-gated and several guessed direct-PDF-host URLs (university course mirrors) returned 404 or timed out; relied instead on CCRMA's secondary literature, which describes and cites it. findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete for both instruments in this family (vl1, karplus) -- 2-4 sources visited per instrument, license called on each, voice structure compared to the module's stated MAX_VOICES for both.

Durable method discoveries for docs/agent-knowledge/instrument-sources.md (not written this run per override; Brad/fleet should land these):

1. WebSearch was unavailable for this entire session -- every call returned 'this session has used its web search budget (200 of 200 WebSearch calls)' before I had made a single successful query. Station A researchers should expect to fall back to WebFetch on directly-targeted URLs plus raw curl, and flag this upstream if it recurs.

2. Wikipedia raw wikitext (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=<Title>&action=raw), fetched with curl and read with grep -n, gives precise, line-numbered, quotable text and surfaces the exact <ref> citations for a claim. This is more trustworthy than asking WebFetch to 'describe' a rendered article, which sometimes paraphrases loosely -- worth using whenever a specific factual claim (e.g. a voice count) needs to be pinned to an exact sentence.

3. GitHub's raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch>/LICENSE plus api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/contents/<dir>, fetched via curl, reliably pulls a project's actual license text and confirms specific source files exist -- faster and more precise than WebFetch's summary of a rendered repo page, and gives an exact license_read_at URL.

4. CCRMA (ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/ and sibling books by Julius O. Smith III) is a rich, freely-readable literature archive for physical-modeling / waveguide / Karplus-Strong math. The text itself is copyright-reserved (not open-licensed), so it is a read-for-math literature source per vision Sec.5, not a portable-code source -- useful for any physical-modeling instrument in this family, not just these two.

5. University of Iowa Electronic Music Studios (theremin.music.uiowa.edu, 'Musical Instrument Samples' database) hosts real single-note captures across strings, winds, brass, percussion and piano at documented pitch/dynamic settings, with an explicit unrestricted-use statement on MIS.html ('may be downloaded and used for any projects, without restrictions'). A reusable capture-tier source anytime a hardware instrument's reference target is an acoustic instrument it imitates or samples.

6. web.archive.org is unreachable via the WebFetch tool entirely (it refuses the host outright); the archive.org Wayback 'available' JSON API is reachable via curl but returned HTTP 429 on every attempt this run. Budget retries/backoff, or a different fetch path, if an archived page is load-bearing for a future dossier.

7. Bing and DuckDuckGo search-result pages, fetched directly via WebFetch, were unreliable in this environment: DuckDuckGo threw a CAPTCHA interstitial every time, and Bing returned an apparently cached/irrelevant result set unrelated to the query text. Do not treat scraped search-engine pages as a WebSearch substitute; go straight to known-good domains (Wikipedia, GitHub, CCRMA, manufacturer/archive sites) instead.

8. soundonsound.com's pre-2000s article archive has been reorganized: old direct article URLs (soundonsound.com/sos/<year>_articles/...) now 302-redirect to a generic 'SOS past articles now online' landing page rather than the article itself. Treat any pre-2010 SOS URL found in a citation as likely dead until reconfirmed live.

findings.method_notes:
Outcome: findings complete for all five electromechanical-piano instruments (rhodes, wurlitzer, pianet, clavinet, cp70) — 4 gold, 1 literature (clavinet, argued down for lack of a reachable hardware capture). Read docs/accuracy-vision.md §3-§5 and docs/accuracy-roadmap.md §3 before starting, per the charter. No files written this run, per the override; all findings are in the structured return.

Durable method discoveries for docs/agent-knowledge/instrument-sources.md (not written this run, per override — hand these to whoever next updates that module):

1. **WebSearch was exhausted before this session's first query** ("200 of 200" already used) — every WebSearch call this run failed immediately. Worth flagging upstream if this recurs; it forced the workaround below.
2. **DAFx paper-archive has an undocumented JSON search API** that is far more reliable than WebFetch-scraping the site: `curl "https://www.dafx.de/paper-archive/api/v1/search?q=<term>&w=anywhere&s=relevance&page=1"` returns JSON hits with title/year/city/filename/authors/abstract; the PDF is then at `https://www.dafx.de/paper-archive/<filename>`. No API key needed. DAFx papers themselves carry no visible license/copyright statement in-text or on the site — treat as "license unverified / academic all-rights-reserved," fine for literature-tier math-derivation, not for redistribution.
3. **archive.org's advancedsearch.php + metadata JSON APIs** are the fastest way to locate and license-check scanned service manuals: `curl --get "https://archive.org/advancedsearch.php" --data-urlencode "q=<terms>" --data-urlencode "fl[]=identifier" --data-urlencode "fl[]=title" --data-urlencode "output=json"` to find an identifier, then `https://archive.org/metadata/<identifier>` for the `licenseurl`/`rights`/`collection` fields — that is the actual license call, not the item's "collection" name. Most manuals on there have `licenseurl: None` (unverified/all-rights-reserved); a minority (e.g. the 1979 Rhodes manual) carry an explicit CC license.
4. **Pianobook (pianobook.co.uk)** is a large free community sample-pack site specifically for acoustic/electromechanical keyboards (piano, Rhodes, Wurlitzer, Pianet, etc.) — its site-wide terms live at `https://www.pianobook.co.uk/faq/` ("copyright free... used... on any commercial and non-commercial compositions"; redistributing the library itself is forbidden). `/faqs/` (plural) 404s — the working page is `/faq/` singular. Per-pack recording-chain documentation (mic/preamp/settings) varies widely pack to pack; check each individually before calling `known_settings=true`. Downloads are gated behind a free account login not exercised this session.
5. **GitHub's REST search API** (`api.github.com/search/repositories?q=...`) surfaces hobbyist hardware-preservation and schematic repos, and permissively-licensed real-hardware sample libraries (e.g. CC BY sfz/FLAC mirrors), that generic web search would likely miss. Unauthenticated rate limits are tight (10 req/min on `/search/*`, 60 req/hour overall) — check `https://api.github.com/rate_limit` and back off with an until-loop rather than guessing. One repo found this way (`sfzinstruments/GregSullivan.E-Pianos`) is a genuinely valuable, CC BY 3.0-licensed, real-hardware multisample library covering three different instrument families at once (Yamaha CP80, Hohner Pianet T, Wurlitzer EP200) — worth remembering for any future electromechanical-keyboard survey.
6. DuckDuckGo's HTML endpoint returns a CAPTCHA to WebFetch; Bing's HTML endpoint returns generic homepage results ignoring the query. Neither is a usable WebSearch substitute via WebFetch — the curl-based API approaches above were the effective fallback.
